Entrepreneurial Finance

Venture financing, term sheets, cap tables, startup valuation, and investor economics.

Lesson Lectures · learn

The entrepreneurship module taught you what to build and why investors write checks. This lesson is about how the money actually works once those checks arrive: the arithmetic of ownership, the contracts that govern who gets paid first, and the slow, predictable erosion of a founder's stake across five rounds of funding. Every number here has a direct consequence for control, incentives, and who walks away rich (or empty-handed) at exit. If you can't read a cap table or spot a punitive liquidation preference, you are negotiating blind.

1 · Pre-money vs. post-money -- the split that sets the price

The single most important equation in venture financing is also the simplest. When an investor offers you $2M at a $8M pre-money valuation, you are selling exactly 20% of your company -- and many first-time founders don't realize it until the paperwork is signed.

Post-money = Pre-money + New investment  ·  Investor ownership = Investment ÷ Post-money

Worked example. Founders have built a product with real traction. A VC offers $2M at an $8M pre-money valuation.

Post-money = $8M + $2M = $10M. The investor owns $2M / $10M = 20%. Founders retain 80%.

If the same investor offered $2M at a $10M pre-money instead, post-money would be $12M and the investor would own only 16.7%. That $2M difference in pre-money valuation just saved the founders 3.3 percentage points of ownership -- worth millions at exit.

The post-money SAFE trap

Y Combinator's post-money SAFE (the standard since 2018) sets the cap as the post-money valuation, meaning the investor's ownership percentage is locked at signing: Investment / Cap = ownership. If you raise $500K on a $5M post-money cap, you have sold exactly 10% -- and every additional SAFE dollar at the same cap stacks on top, diluting you further before a single priced round happens. Many founders treat the cap as a pre-money number by habit and miscalculate their dilution by 15-25%.

3 · Cap table mechanics -- founding through Series B

A cap table is not a static document. It is a living record that changes with every round, every option grant, and every conversion. Walk through three stages of a company called Relay and watch how the founders' stake shrinks while the pie grows. Click each bar segment.

Notice what happened to the seed investor: they went from 20% to 13.1% without selling a single share. That is passive dilution -- the same mechanic that erodes founder stakes. Pro rata rights exist precisely to let investors fight this by writing follow-on checks.

4 · SAFEs and convertible notes -- the bridge instruments

Before a startup is ready for a priced round with a formal valuation, it raises money using instruments that promise future equity. The two dominant forms: SAFEs (Y Combinator's invention, no interest, no maturity) and convertible notes (actual debt with interest and a due date). Both convert into preferred stock at the next priced round.

Conversion price = min(Cap ÷ Pre-money shares,  Round price × (1 - Discount))

Investors get the better of the two calculations. The cap protects them if the valuation skyrockets; the discount rewards them for early risk if it doesn't.

Conversion math. An angel invests $200K via a SAFE with a $4M cap and a 20% discount. At Series A, the company prices at $10M pre-money with 10M shares outstanding.

Cap path: Conversion price = $4M / 10M shares = $0.40/share. Shares received = $200K / $0.40 = 500,000 shares.

Discount path: Series A price = $10M / 10M = $1.00/share. Discounted = $1.00 x 0.80 = $0.80/share. Shares = $200K / $0.80 = 250,000 shares.

The cap path yields more shares, so the investor converts at $0.40. They effectively bought in at a $4M valuation while Series A investors paid $10M -- the reward for taking early risk.

Unlike a SAFE, a convertible note has a maturity date (typically 18-24 months). If you haven't raised a priced round by then, the note holder can technically demand repayment -- and if you can't pay, they can force a bankruptcy proceeding. In practice most note holders extend the maturity, but it gives them leverage in negotiations. Notes also accrue interest (typically 2-8% annually), which adds to the principal that converts into shares, creating extra dilution. A $500K note at 6% over 2 years becomes $561,800 at conversion.

5 · Term sheet anatomy -- the terms that actually matter

A term sheet is 5-10 pages. Most of it is boilerplate. The terms below are where founders win or lose control and economics. Click each to understand the mechanic.

1x non-participating (standard, founder-friendly): the investor gets their money back OR converts to common and shares pro rata -- whichever is higher. In a big exit, they convert. In a small exit, they take their money back and the common holders split what's left. Participating preferred (investor-friendly, sometimes called "double dip"): the investor gets their money back AND shares pro rata in the remainder. This means they effectively get paid twice. A 2x participating preference on a $5M investment requires $10M off the top before anyone else sees a dime, plus a share of everything after.

Both protect investors in a down round by adjusting their conversion price downward. Broad-based weighted average (standard): the conversion price is adjusted using a formula that accounts for how much money was raised at the lower price and the total shares outstanding. The more money raised at the lower price, the bigger the adjustment. Full ratchet (aggressive): the conversion price drops to match the new, lower price -- regardless of how little was raised at that price. If a Series A investor paid $2.00/share and a small bridge round prices at $0.50, full ratchet reprices all their shares to $0.50, massively diluting founders. Avoid full ratchet.

A typical seed-stage board is 2 founders + 0 investors (or 2+1). By Series A, a standard board is 2 founders + 1 lead investor + 0-1 independent = 3-4 seats. By Series B, it often shifts to 2+2+1, and founders can lose board control. The board approves budgets, hires/fires the CEO, approves fundraising, and decides on exits. Board control is separate from share ownership -- you can own 51% of the company and still be fired by a board you don't control.

Even without board control, preferred shareholders typically hold veto rights over specific actions: issuing new shares, selling the company, taking on debt, changing the charter, or increasing the option pool. These are protective provisions -- a checklist of things the company cannot do without investor consent, regardless of who controls the board. They are standard and generally reasonable, but aggressive investors sometimes expand them to cover hiring, spending, or pivoting.

6 · The liquidation waterfall -- who gets paid, and in what order

When a company exits, cash does not flow evenly to all shareholders. It cascades through a hierarchy of preferences. Walk through a $50M acquisition of a company with $5M in Series A (1x non-participating) and $15M in Series B (1x non-participating), with founders and employees holding common stock.

When the waterfall drowns the founders

Now imagine that same company with participating preferred on the Series B. Series B takes their $15M preference AND 30% of the remaining $35M = $10.5M, for a total of $25.5M. Series A takes $5M + 12% of $30M = $8.6M. Founders and employees split what's left: $15.9M -- nearly half what they'd get under non-participating terms. Participating preferred is the single most expensive economic term a founder can agree to.

7 · Dilution math -- from 100% to 8%

Every founder starts at 100%. Here is a realistic walk through how that number shrinks. Follow the math -- each step is a real mechanism, not a simplification.

Founding (100%) → Co-founder split (50%) → Option pool (42.5%) → Seed (34%) → Series A (24%) → Series B (17%) → Series C (12%) → More options (8-10%)

Step by step for one co-founder:

Day 0: You own 100%. You bring on a co-founder and split 50/50. You now own 50%.

Seed: You create a 15% option pool (from your shares, not the investor's) and sell 20% to a seed investor. Your 50% is diluted by (1 - 0.15) x (1 - 0.20) = 0.68 of its pre-round value = 34%.

Series A: A new 5% option pool top-up and 25% to the Series A lead. Your 34% x (1 - 0.05) x (1 - 0.25) = 24.2%.

Series B: 20% to Series B investors, 5% option pool refresh. Your 24.2% x 0.95 x 0.80 = 18.4%.

Series C + option grants: Another 20% round plus option exercise and secondary sales. A single founder holding 8-12% at IPO is standard for a venture-backed company. Mark Zuckerberg retained 28% at Facebook's IPO -- an outlier achieved through supervoting shares and unusual leverage.

Investors routinely insist that the option pool be created before their money enters the cap table -- carved from the pre-money valuation. This means the dilution from the option pool falls entirely on existing shareholders (founders), not on the new investor. If a VC offers $5M at $15M pre-money but requires a 15% option pool, the effective pre-money for existing shareholders is $15M x (1 - 0.15) = $12.75M. The advertised $15M pre-money is a fiction -- the real founder-relevant valuation is $12.75M. Always compute the effective pre-money after the pool carve-out.

8 · Venture debt and alternatives to equity

Not every dollar of startup funding needs to come with dilution. Three instruments sit between pure equity and pure bootstrapping:

Venture debt is a loan to a VC-backed company, typically sized at 25-50% of the last equity round. It comes with interest (Prime + 2-5%), a repayment schedule (36 months is typical), and a small warrant giving the lender the right to buy equity (usually 0.5-2% of the company). Use it to: (1) extend runway by 3-6 months without dilution, (2) finance specific capital expenditures (equipment, inventory), (3) bridge to profitability when you're close. Do NOT use it when: revenue is unpredictable, burn is accelerating, or you might need the covenant flexibility that equity provides. Silicon Valley Bank (before its collapse), Western Technology Investment, and Lighter Capital were major venture lenders.

You receive a lump sum and repay a fixed multiple (typically 1.3-2x) as a percentage of monthly revenue (5-10%). If revenue drops, payments shrink; if it grows, you repay faster. Zero dilution, no board seats, no personal guarantees. Best for SaaS and e-commerce companies with predictable monthly revenue above $10K+. Firms like Pipe, Clearco, and Capchase popularized this from 2019 onward. The effective APR can be high (15-40%) if you repay quickly, but many founders accept that to avoid giving up equity.

Debt has a fixed obligation: you must repay regardless of outcome. If a startup takes $3M in venture debt and then misses its growth targets, the debt covenants can trigger default. The lender can call the loan, seize assets, or force a fire sale -- outcomes that equity investors never impose. The 2023 SVB collapse showed this systemically: startups that had concentrated their venture debt and banking with one institution faced existential risk when that institution failed. Rule of thumb: venture debt should extend a clear path, never substitute for one.

9 · Case study -- NovaChem from pre-seed to Series B

NovaChem is a composite case based on real biotech and climate-tech financing patterns. Follow the economics through three rounds.

Pre-seed (2021): Two founders, 10M shares each (20M total). They raise $500K via post-money SAFE at a $5M cap. The SAFE holders will own 10% at conversion ($500K / $5M).

Seed (2022): A VC leads a $3M priced seed at $12M pre-money. Before the round, the board creates a 10% option pool (from pre-money). The SAFE converts: $500K / $5M cap = 10% of post-money shares. Post-money = $12M + $3M = $15M. Seed investor owns 20%. SAFE holders own ~10%. Option pool: ~10%. Founders' combined stake: ~60%, or 30% each.

Series A (2024): NovaChem has $2M ARR growing 3x. A top-tier firm leads $15M at $45M pre-money. Option pool topped up to 12%. Post-money = $60M. Series A gets 25%. Founders are now at ~20% combined (10% each). Seed investor diluted from 20% to ~15%. But everyone's shares are worth more: the seed investor's 15% of $60M = $9M, a 3x on $3M invested.

The math check: Founder A's 10% of $60M = $6M in paper value. They started with 50% of a company worth nothing. They now own 10% of a company worth $60M. That is the core trade of venture financing -- smaller percentage of a much larger number.

10 · Check yourself

A startup raises $3M at a $12M pre-money valuation. What percentage does the investor own?

Post-money = $12M + $3M = $15M. Investor ownership = $3M / $15M = 20%. The denominator is always post-money, not pre-money.

An angel invests $100K on a SAFE with a $5M cap. At Series A, the company is valued at $20M pre-money with 10M shares outstanding. What conversion price does the angel get?

Cap conversion price = $5M / 10M shares = $0.50/share. Series A price = $20M / 10M = $2.00. The angel gets the lower price ($0.50), yielding 200,000 shares instead of 50,000.

In a $30M exit, a Series A investor holds 1x non-participating preferred with a $5M investment and owns 20% of the company. What do they choose?

Non-participating means they choose the higher of preference ($5M) or conversion (20% x $30M = $6M). They convert. The third option describes participating preferred -- a different, more investor-friendly term.

A VC offers $5M at $15M pre-money but requires a 15% option pool created before pricing. What is the effective pre-money for existing shareholders?

The 15% option pool is carved from pre-money: $15M x (1 - 0.15) = $12.75M effective pre-money. The $15M headline valuation obscures $2.25M of founder dilution.

What is the key difference between a SAFE and a convertible note?

A convertible note accrues interest and has a maturity date -- it is legally debt that converts to equity. A SAFE has no interest, no maturity, and no repayment obligation. Neither typically carries board seats at the seed stage.

Your move

Build a cap table in a spreadsheet for a fictional company from founding through Series B. Start with 10M shares, add a 10% option pool and a $2M seed round, then a $10M Series A. Compute every shareholder's percentage at each stage. Then model a $40M exit under both 1x non-participating and 1x participating preferred -- the difference in founder payout is the cost of one term sheet line item.
